'''Janet Gretchen Osteryoung''' (March 1, 1939 – September 21, 2021) was an American chemist who was the director of the Chemistry Division of the [[National Science Foundation]] from 1994 to 2001. Her research furthered the development of electroanalysis and especially that of [[squarewave voltammetry|square wave voltammetry]]. She was elected a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1984 and awarded the [[Garvan–Olin Medal]] in 1987.

== Early life and education ==
Janet Gretchen Jones was born in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], and grew up in [[Vero Beach, Florida]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Obituary. Janet Jones |url=https://www.floridatoday.com/obituaries/bft077403|access-date=2021-10-12|website=www.floridatoday.com|language=en}}</ref> She was an undergraduate student at [[Swarthmore College]], where she was a Merit scholar.<ref name=":4">{{cite newsletter|title=Kudos|journal=SEACcommunications|url=https://seac.online/seac-newsletter/issue-archive/|volume=13|issue=1|date=December 1996}}</ref> Jones was a graduate student at [[California Institute of Technology]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Janet Gretchen Osteryoung|language=English|oclc=4778468233}}</ref> where she worked alongside Fred Anson on ligand bridging in charge transfer reactions.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Ligand bridging in the oxidation of chromium(II) at mercury electrodes|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechETD:etd-09232002-120547|date=1967|language=English|first=Janet Gretchen|last=Jones}}</ref> Robert Osteryoung was a Visiting Associate in the Department of Chemistry at Caltech at this same time. After marrying, Janet and Robert Osteryoung both continued to carry out research in the field of electroanalytical chemistry.

== Research and career ==
Osteryoung was appointed to the faculty at [[Montana State University]] in 1967.<ref name=":0" /> She moved to [[Colorado State University]] a year later, where she worked in the Departments of Civil Engineering and Microbiology.<ref name=":0" /> In 1977, Osteryoung moved to the [[National Science Foundation]], where she was the program director for chemical analysis.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Janet Osteryoung - UB People - University Archives - University at Buffalo Libraries|url=https://library.buffalo.edu/archives/ubpeople/detail.html?ID=2936|access-date=2021-10-10|website=library.buffalo.edu}}</ref>

Osteryoung was made associate professor at the [[State University of New York at Buffalo]] in 1979 and professor in 1982. In 1985 Osteryoung was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] and spent a year at the [[University of Southampton]], where she investigated the fundamentals of solid electrodes.<ref name=":3" />

Osteryoung moved to [[North Carolina State University]] in 1992, where she served as head of department for two years.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Faculty, Staff and Administration|url=https://projects.ncsu.edu/ncsu/chancellor_report/faculty/faculty-bar.html|access-date=2021-10-10|website=projects.ncsu.edu|archive-date=2021-10-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211010214424/https://projects.ncsu.edu/ncsu/chancellor_report/faculty/faculty-bar.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1994, she returned to the National Science Foundation, where she was made director of the division of chemistry. She was the first woman to win the Jacob F. Schoellkopf medal in 1992.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=JACOB F. SCHOELLKOPF Medal|url=https://wnyacs.files.wordpress.com/2019/08/schoellkhist.pdf}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Janet Jones was once married to Robert Osteryoung, who was also an award-winning chemist.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stojek|first=Zbigniew|date=2005|title=Guest Editorial. Robert A. Osteryoung (1927–2004)|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/elan.200590015|journal=Electroanalysis|language=en|volume=17|issue=15–16|pages=1339–1340|doi=10.1002/elan.200590015|issn=1521-4109|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In April 2010, she married Chris Cobb in Washington, D.C.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=A Gift Grounded in Love and Advocacy|url=https://news.syr.edu/blog/2020/09/02/a-gift-grounded-in-love-and-advocacy|access-date=2021-10-12|website=news.syr.edu|date=2 September 2020 |language=en}}</ref> Together, Jones and Cobb established the Comis Foundation, a family philanthropic foundation to benefit children and youth.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Comis Foundation |url=https://comisfoundation.org|access-date=2021-10-12|website=comisfoundation.org|language=en}}</ref>
